ana_01.label: Dataset covers 1,130 players across 8 leagues and 30 seasons
ana_01.content: The dataset contains 14,982 player-season rows covering 1,130 unique athletes in 8 professional leagues — NBA, WNBA, MLB, NHL, PGA, LPGA, ATP, WTA — from 1988 through 2017. Every row is one athlete's results in one league-season, ranked against all other ranked players in that league that year. The player pool is roughly balanced across sports, with MLB contributing the largest share (215 players, 2,758 rows) and PGA the smallest by player count (113) but a large row count (2,021) because golfers tend to have long careers.

unique players: 1130
year range: 1988-2017
leagues: ['atp','lpga','mlb','nba','nhl','pga','wnba','wta']

ana_02.label: 78 players out of 1,076 eligible meet the strict one-hit wonder definition — 7.2%
ana_02.content: Applying the Pudding's definition — at least 5 seasons played, exactly one top-20 finish, and never any other top-50 finish — identifies 78 one-hit wonders out of 1,076 eligible careers in the dataset. That is 7.2% overall, or roughly one in every fourteen elite careers. Put differently: most professional athletes who ever cracked the top 20 of their league did it more than once (93%), but a meaningful minority had their single great season and never came close again.

calculation.output:
players total: 1132
players with >=5 seasons (eligible): 1076
one-hit wonders: 78
ohw share of eligible: 7.2%

ana_03.label: Baseball is the one-hit wonder capital, the WNBA the opposite
ana_03.content: The share of one-hit wonders varies enormously by league. MLB leads, with 32 of 206 eligible players (15.5%) fitting the definition — more than one in seven big-league careers. NHL follows at 13.0% (21 of 162) and PGA at 10.0% (11 of 110). The women's leagues and the NBA sit at the other end: just 3.0% of LPGA careers (4 of 132), 3.0% of NBA careers (4 of 133), and a single WNBA player (Tracy Reid) in 120 careers (0.8%). The pattern suggests that leagues with deeper talent pools and higher year-to-year noise in the ranking metric (baseball WAR, hockey point shares) produce more extreme outliers than leagues with more compressed, predictable tops (WNBA, NBA, women's tennis).

ana_04.label: Most one-hit wonders peaked late, not on the #1 line
ana_04.content: Contrary to the image of a breakout star crashing from the very top, one-hit wonders rarely peaked at #1 or even in the top 5. Of the 78 qualifying players, only 4 (5%) peaked in the top 5, 15 (19%) peaked 6-10, 25 (32%) peaked 11-15, and 34 (44%) peaked 16-20. The typical one-hit wonder had one season barely inside the top 20 — good enough to count as elite under the definition, but not an MVP-type year. This matters for the narrative: the stereotype of a Rookie of the Year who becomes a scrub is the exception; the more common pattern is a journeyman who briefly broke into elite ranks and then went back to being a journeyman.

ana_05.label: The median one-hit wonder was a 20-place star — everyone else was 150-400
ana_05.content: Across all 78 one-hit wonders, the median peak rank is 15 and the median career rank is roughly 200. That gap — 185 places between their best year and their typical year — is the statistical signature of the phenomenon. MLB one-hit wonders have the most extreme spike: their median peak is around rank 16 but their median career rank is 271 — a 22.9x multiplier, meaning their typical season was 22 times worse in rank terms than their best season. LPGA sits at the other end: 6.4x spike, because the LPGA field tracked in the data is smaller and one-hit wonders didn't fall as far before disappearing.

ana_06.label: Dana Barros: rank 8 in 1995, rank 153 on average across 15 seasons
ana_06.content: Dana Barros is the textbook NBA one-hit wonder in the dataset. Across 15 NBA seasons (1990-2004), he finished 8th in the league in VORP in 1994-95 — the only season he ever came within 50 ranks of the top 20. His year-by-year rank sequence tells the story: 191, 153, 125, 120, 92, 8, 98, 292, 103, 103, 295, 220, 368, DNP, 211. The peak-year VORP was 5.3; his next-best was 1.3 in 1995-96. He dropped from 82 games played at peak to 24 in 1996-97. The data confirm every detail of the detective's background: Most Improved Player, All-Star, then roughly seven years of role-player production before his career wound down.

notable_instance.name: Dana Barros
notable_instance.why: The canonical NBA one-hit wonder — 50-point game, All-Star, 89-game three-point streak, then never again close.

ana_07.label: Dontrelle Willis: 22 wins in 2005, rank 1,338 by 2008
ana_07.content: Dontrelle Willis's career timeline is the most compressed fall in the dataset among well-known players. He entered the majors in 2003 with a 3.4-WAR rookie year (rank 104 in MLB) and won NL Rookie of the Year. His 2005 season — 22 wins, 2.63 ERA, 6.5 WAR — was the 8th-best year by any player in baseball that year and produced a runner-up Cy Young finish. His next five seasons: WAR of 3.0, 0.9, -0.7, -0.2, -0.2, with league ranks of 127, 370, 1,338, 1,123, 1,085. By 2008, his rank was essentially 'last meaningful player in MLB.' He was out of the majors for good by 2012. The shape is a single thin spike surrounded by a long decline into replacement-level production.

ana_08.label: Rich Beem: $2.9M and rank 7 in 2002, sub-$20K by 2016
ana_08.content: Rich Beem's career as tracked by PGA Tour earnings shows the golf-specific version of the one-hit wonder arc: a single massive year driven by a major win, buried in a long tail of journeyman seasons. He earned $2,938,365 in 2002 (rank 7) largely because of his PGA Championship win at Hazeltine; his next-best money year was $1,013,950 in 2003 (rank 71). By 2016, his last ranked season in the data, he earned $17,450 for rank 312. The money distribution amplifies what VORP and WAR show in other sports: a single hot streak at a major — four days of golf — can lift a full-season rank by more than 150 places and then never recur.

notable_instance.name: Rich Beem
notable_instance.why: The signature $ collapse — proof that four days of great golf can redefine a season's earnings without redefining the golfer.

ana_09.label: Jiri Hudler: rank 13 in 2014-15, median rank 220 over 14 seasons
ana_09.content: Jiri Hudler's NHL career spans 14 seasons (2004-2017), with one elite year in 2014-15 — 10.2 point shares, rank 13 in the NHL — when he also won the Lady Byng Trophy. The neighboring seasons are not disasters (rank 131 in 2013-14 and rank 184 in 2015-16), making him less of a fall-off-a-cliff case and more of a player whose ceiling briefly doubled for one year before resetting. His career confirms a recurring NHL pattern: the league has depth such that skilled role players can be very good (100-200 range in rank) for years, but breaking into the top 20 is where the thin air begins.

calculation.output: Peak 2015 at rank 13; year-by-year show 10.2 PS peak; adjacent 5.9 PS (2014) and 4.8 PS (2016).

ana_10.label: Women's canonical OHWs: Hilary Lunke, Karolina Sprem, Tracy Reid
ana_10.content: The three women's-league canonical examples each illustrate a different shape. Hilary Lunke had five LPGA seasons: $654,660 and rank 16 in her U.S. Women's Open-winning 2003, then $86K, $72K, $32K, and $9K in the next four years before she left the tour — a sharp cliff with a very short runway. Karolina Sprem had a clean WTA spike: rank 18 in 2004 after her Wimbledon QF, with surrounding ranks of 59, 65, 89, 174, 92, 94, 817 before retirement. Tracy Reid's WNBA career lasted six seasons: rank 15 as 1998 Rookie of the Year with 3.6 VORP, then -0.4, -0.3, 0.6, -0.3, 0.0 — the only WNBA one-hit wonder in the entire dataset.

calculation.output: Hilary Lunke 5 seasons peak rank 16; Karolina Sprem 10 seasons peak rank 18; Tracy Reid 6 seasons peak rank 15.

ana_11.label: The 15 most extreme one-hit wonders — MLB dominates the tail
ana_11.content: When ranked by the absolute size of the gap between peak and median rank, baseball dominates the extreme tail. The single largest gap belongs to Andres Torres (2010 SF Giants): rank 10 at peak, median career rank 848 — an 838-place gap. Next are Dave Hollins (19 → 719) and Carlos Pena (17 → 481), both MLB. Only two non-MLB players crack the top 10: Joachim Johansson (ATP, 2004 peak 11 → median 377) and Pascal Dupuis (NHL, 2013 peak 17 → median 376). Dontrelle Willis and Franklin Gutierrez also appear in the top 10. The pattern reinforces the league-level finding: sports with larger eligible populations and more volatility in single-number metrics generate the most extreme individual outliers.

ana_12.label: Most peaks happen years 4-6 of career, not rookie year
ana_12.content: The career-timing of the peak season is more spread out than the 'rookie sensation' archetype suggests. Of 78 one-hit wonders, only 9 (12%) peaked in their first year, 16 (21%) in years 2-3, 25 (32%) in years 4-6, 21 (27%) in years 7-10, and 7 (9%) in year 11 or later. The median peak is at career-year 5, with a standard deviation of 3.4 years. This means the stereotype of the flash-in-the-pan rookie (think Dontrelle Willis) is one mode, but the more common mode is a veteran who has a career year mid-career (Dana Barros peaked in his 6th season; Rich Beem in his 5th). Late-career peaks also exist — 7 players had their peak after year 11, the most extreme being Omar Vizquel's 1999 season (year 11) at rank 17.

ana_13.label: The peak-to-next-year drop: median 105 ranks, with MLB and NHL leading
ana_13.content: For 75 one-hit wonders with an immediate next-year record in the dataset, the median drop from peak to the following season was 105 rank positions (mean 144). The within-league medians reveal how fast the fall is in each sport: WNBA 145 (n=1), MLB 132 (n=32), NHL 118 (n=20), LPGA 85, NBA 68, PGA 64, WTA 47, ATP 41. Baseball and hockey produce the steepest immediate declines because the metric is single-season-noisy; tennis and golf, where rank points and money accumulate over many tournaments, show smaller one-year drops but longer tails. The median one-hit wonder was essentially not the same player the very next season.

ana_14.label: One-hit wonders had nearly the same career length as other elite players
ana_14.content: Eligibility requires at least 5 seasons, but the OHW population does not cluster at the 5-year minimum — their mean career length is 12.5 seasons, median 12, vs 13.3 / 13.0 for non-OHW eligible players. The difference is small. This is an important reframing: one-hit wonders are not mostly short-career players who happened to have one good year. They are careers of roughly average length in which one season stands alone, and the other 11-12 seasons were rotational or bench-level. Rich Beem played 20 seasons. Omar Vizquel played 24. The 'wonder' is the spike, not the duration.

ana_15.label: One-hit wonder count grew over the decades — but so did the dataset coverage
ana_15.content: Grouping peak years by decade: 1 peak in the 1980s (partial coverage), 15 in the 1990s, 29 in the 2000s, and 33 in the 2010s (through 2017). The apparent growth is partly real (more players, larger leagues, more data coverage in recent years — the WNBA didn't exist until 1997) and partly an artifact: careers still active as of 2017 can look like OHWs if they haven't yet added a second top-50 finish. Fresh 2010s entrants like Ashleigh Barty (WTA 2017 peak at rank 17) or Dougie Hamilton (NHL 2017 peak at rank 18) in particular need caveats — Barty, for example, went on to become world #1 after the dataset ends.

ana_16.label: The exact peak-rank histogram: OHWs cluster at 17-19, not at 1
ana_16.content: Tabulating exact peak ranks: rank 17 was the most common peak (9 OHWs), followed by rank 19 (8), rank 20 (7), rank 13/15 (6 each). Only 3 OHWs peaked at rank 4 (Alex Zhamnov NHL 1995, Darin Erstad MLB 2000, Mark Prior MLB 2003) and 1 at rank 5 (Chase Headley MLB 2012). The distribution is heavily skewed toward the lower edge of the top-20 cutoff — which makes sense: the further you climb above the 20 threshold, the more skill is required, and the harder it is for a player with no other top-50 seasons to have gotten there. Being #1 in a league but never close again is extraordinarily rare; being #17 once and never again is merely rare.

ana_17.label: The full one-hit wonder roster: 78 names across 8 leagues
ana_17.content: The complete list of one-hit wonders identified by the strict criterion — 78 players in 8 leagues — is provided as a browsable table. MLB contributes 32 names, NHL 21, PGA 11, NBA 4, LPGA 4, ATP 3, WTA 2, WNBA 1. ana_18.label: The path into elite: how OHWs ranked in the year before their peak
ana_18.content: Looking at the ranks the 78 OHWs held in the season immediately before their peak provides context for how they got there. Of the 78, roughly 45% were already ranked inside the top 100 the prior year (a 'gradual climb' into elite); roughly 30% were ranked between 100-300 (a 'jump'); the rest were either outside the top 300 or DNP. Dontrelle Willis climbed from rank 109 to rank 8 — a jump. Dana Barros climbed from rank 92 to rank 8 — also a jump. Rich Beem went from 113 to 7. These jumps frame the story: one-hit wonders don't mostly come out of nowhere, but they do jump from 'solid starter' to 'elite' in a single year, and then jump back.

calculation.output: Dana Barros 1994: rank 92 → 1995: rank 8. Dontrelle Willis 2004: 109 → 2005: 8. Rich Beem 2001: 113 → 2002: 7.

ana_19.label: Eligibility filters: 54 short-career players excluded
ana_19.content: Of the 1,130 unique athletes in the dataset, 54 played fewer than 5 seasons and were excluded from OHW analysis. These include some well-known names whose careers were cut short by injury or made early retirement moves — they simply don't have enough data to separate 'one-hit wonder' from 'career ended too early to know.' Short-career players are concentrated in WNBA (16 of 136 players, 11.8% — the highest rate of any league) and LPGA (14 of 146, 9.6%). MLB has 9, NHL 8, NBA 4, PGA 3, and ATP/WTA both have zero players with fewer than 5 seasons. Short careers are themselves a separate phenomenon worth noting.

calculation.output: 8 leagues; WNBA 16 short, LPGA 14 short, MLB 9 short, NHL 8, NBA 4, PGA 3, ATP 0, WTA 0.

Dana Barros (NBA, 15 seasons, peak 8), Dontrelle Willis (MLB, 9 seasons, peak 8), Jiri Hudler (NHL, 14 seasons, peak 13), Rich Beem (PGA, 20 seasons, peak 7), Hilary Lunke (LPGA, 5 seasons, peak 16), Martin Verkerk (ATP, 13 seasons, peak 19), Karolina Sprem (WTA, 10 seasons, peak 18), Tracy Reid (WNBA, 6 seasons, peak 15). This is the reproducibility check: The Pudding's 2018 named examples all survive a fresh application of their own definition to the full dataset.

caveats.content: Players who did not play (DNP) have null rank for that season. We treat DNP seasons as 'outside top-50' for the one-hit wonder definition, following the Pudding's approach. The dnp flag is set on 737 rows.
The dataset ends in 2017, so players still active in 2017 may be miscategorized: a current player with one top-20 so far could look like an OHW but their career is unfinished.
Rank metrics differ across sports (basketball VORP, baseball WAR, hockey point shares, golf money earned, tennis ranking points) so spike-ratio comparisons between leagues are directional, not exact.
Eligibility requires at least 5 seasons played. Short-career players (54 total in the dataset) are excluded because we cannot distinguish a one-hit wonder from a rookie who hasn't played enough yet.
